\# & Established by prior art & \textbf{What this paper adds}, and the evidence \\
\midrule
1 & Exact fANOVA on complete grids: to order eleven on AutoML loss landscapes~\cite{pushak2022automl}, to order two on one architecture grid~\cite{klein2019tabular}; the categorical closed form in full generality~\cite{ferrere2026exact}. & \textbf{The amplitude spectrum of a NAS landscape, measured exactly.} The same decomposition turned on NAS landscapes, where the answer was not foregone: it makes AutoML landscapes \emph{high}-order and both NAS spaces low-order. The apparatus is borrowed; the measurement and its consequences are not. \emph{order $\le 2$ carries 67.9--88.2\% of accuracy variance, order $\le 3$ carries 93.4--96.7\%.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
2 & Cheap predictors are rarely beaten~\cite{white2021powerful,ning2021evaluating} and some ruggedness is seed noise~\cite{white2021exploring}; neither is a limit. & \textbf{A structural ceiling on any degree-$d$ predictor.} A limit rather than a comparison: because the components are orthogonal, the cumulative spectrum caps the $R^{2}$ of \emph{any} degree-$d$ function, however much data it is given. \emph{degree-2 ceiling 0.68--0.88; degree-3 ceiling 0.93--0.97.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
3 & On this space correlation length grows with task difficulty and search is more reliable on harder tasks~\cite{tao2024landscape,lopes2024operation}; no mechanism is offered. & \textbf{The task-dependence of landscape simplicity is an artifact of the scale.} The mechanism, which dissolves the effect: easy tasks are compressed against an accuracy ceiling, a monotone recalibration collapses the three spectra onto one, and where there is no compression it buys almost nothing. \emph{order $\le 2$ goes from 67.9, 78.1, 88.2\% to 89.5, 88.4, 88.0\% after recalibration.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
4 & Fit the prior on the hardest dataset available and transfer it; it outranks the same model fitted on the target's own labels~\cite{tao2024landscape,lopes2024operation}. & \textbf{Recalibrate first; a prior from a harder task mostly supplied a less compressed scale.} True as measured, but mostly a matter of scale: recalibrating the target's own labels beats raw-scale transfer at every budget on both metrics, and recalibrating the source closes most of that gap. \emph{CIFAR-10 at 1{,}000 labels: $\rho=0.935$ recalibrated against 0.879 raw-scale transfer, 0.908 recalibrated transfer and 0.682 raw; regret 0.05 against 0.52, 0.34 and 1.32.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
5 & Protein and RNA fitness functions are Fourier-sparse, so label complexity follows that sparsity rather than the size of the space~\cite{brookes2022sparsity}. & \textbf{Label complexity is a coefficient count, not a function of the space size.} The same bound in NAS, with a consequence that setting does not have: a study that has already run owns the labels a degree-2 model of a $10^{18}$-point space needs. \emph{1{,}514 cells covered at 3.5 and 3.1 labels each, from 0.010\% of the grid.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
6 & Path encodings beat adjacency encodings, justified by relabelling invariance and graceful truncation~\cite{white2020encodings}. & \textbf{The scope boundary is a basis in which the function is not low-order.} The spectral reading: a re-encoding adds no information, it lowers the order, and a held-out $R^{2}$ measures whether it did---so the scope boundary is testable before a budget is spent, and repairable for free. \emph{held-out $R^{2}=-0.10$ on NAS-Bench-101 against $+0.58$ to $+0.84$ elsewhere; re-encoding lifts $\rho$ from 0.499 to 0.692.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
7 & Cheap rankers are compared by rank correlation, one space at a time~\cite{white2021powerful,abdelfattah2021zerocost,shu2022unifying}. & \textbf{Rank correlation and regret at a shortlist disagree.} The two orderings disagree in both directions, so correlation does not answer what a budget asks; we report $k^{\star}$, the smallest shortlist whose regret falls below a tenth of a point. \emph{the surrogate leads in $\rho$ yet $k^{\star}=10$ against $50$ for a measured epoch; on NAS-Bench-201 SynFlow leads the shortlist on two of three datasets.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
8 & A per-space table of which zero-cost proxy wins, computed with the target labels in hand~\cite{krishnakumar2022nasbenchsuitezero,shu2022unifying}. & \textbf{Which free ranker is best is not identifiable without target labels.} That table is an oracle quantity: choosing on the only labels a label-free deployment has costs most of the advantage, so the deployable object is an untuned fusion rather than a choice. \emph{an honest choice gives up $0.89$ points where an oracle gives up $0.21$; the untuned fusion wins by $0.77$.} \\
\addlinespace[2pt]
9 & Price a policy without GPUs by degrading a measured reference to the cheap signal's fidelity~\cite{zela2022surrogate,mehta2022nasbenchsuite}. & \textbf{Emulating a cheap signal by corrupting a reference can invert its conclusion.} The precondition fails where the device is most tempting: inside a model-in-the-loop search the fidelity depends on what the policy measures, so the loop must be refitted and the shortcut inverts its own sign. \emph{a gain predicted against $-6.64$ to $-14.30$ measured, across budgets.} \\
\bottomrule
